doc.title: Elvin Jones — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Qualities of a bandleader
summary: He says a leader needs understanding of people and should not ask what he cannot do himself.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: So throughout your career you worked with some of the most accomplished musicians in this music. Obviously, you’re working with them as a sideman; you’re observing them as a bandleaders. Throughout your career as a bandleader, how were they influential, which ones were influential, and what did they give you, or what did you observe as far as being a bandleader? What are the traits that make a great bandleader, what are the things that you got through other people, or maybe observed from other people?

It’s a great many things, I think it’s more of … you have to have a natural understanding of the basic psychology of people. You know, you don’t scare somebody to death. They might be ready to play but they’re shy. So, it’s just that you have to be able to recognize what it is that that person is saying or representing, and see how truthful he is. You can usually tell if a person is truthful, and that’s enough.

Even though from 1967 on you became a bandleader, yet, you still continued to work on other people’s projects as a collaborator. This is seemingly a very rare and very remarkable gift to be able to be a bandleader and then to adapt and be a in a roll as a sideman or accompanist.
Does this still suit you to this day?
You know, I’ll tell you it’s like they say in the Army, “A good leader wouldn’t tell his men to do something that he couldn’t do himself.” So it’s as simple as that.
